mainEntity.name: Is composite bonding a permanent solution for eroded teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding is not considered a permanent solution. It is a durable cosmetic restoration that can last several years with good oral hygiene and maintenance, but it will likely need to be repaired or replaced over time. The longevity of bonding on eroded teeth also depends on whether the underlying cause of erosion has been addressed. Your dentist can give you a more specific indication based on your individual circumstances during a clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Will composite bonding stop my teeth from eroding further?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding can provide a protective covering over affected tooth surfaces, which may help reduce sensitivity and restore structure. However, it does not address the source of erosion. If the acid cause — whether dietary or related to a medical condition such as reflux — is still present, erosion may continue on other surfaces or around the restoration. Managing the cause of erosion is considered an important part of any long-term treatment plan.

mainEntity.name: Does composite bonding hurt if my teeth are already sensitive?

acceptedAnswer.text: The composite bonding procedure is generally well-tolerated and is typically carried out without the need for local anaesthetic, as it involves minimal tooth preparation. If your teeth are already sensitive due to erosion, your dentist will take this into account and ensure you are comfortable throughout. Any post-treatment sensitivity is usually mild and temporary. If sensitivity persists or worsens after treatment, it is worth contacting your dental practice.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my tooth erosion is mild or more severe?

acceptedAnswer.text: The degree of tooth erosion can only be accurately assessed through a clinical dental examination. A dentist will examine the affected surfaces, evaluate the depth and pattern of wear, and may use indices or photographs to monitor changes over time. Signs that erosion may be more advanced include significant tooth shortening, visible dentine exposure, frequent sensitivity, or changes to the bite. If you are concerned, arranging an appointment for assessment is the most reliable step.

mainEntity.name: Can children or teenagers have composite bonding for eroded teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding may be considered for younger patients in some circumstances, but treatment planning for adolescents requires particularly careful consideration. Teeth in younger patients may still be developing, and the gum line can change over time. A dentist will always carry out a full assessment before recommending any treatment for younger patients and will consider age, dental development, and the cause of erosion as part of their evaluation.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I do not treat mild tooth erosion?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild erosion that is not monitored or managed may gradually progress. As enamel continues to thin, teeth may become increasingly sensitive, more vulnerable to chipping, and the appearance of the smile may change further. Early detection and preventative measures — combined with monitoring by a dental professional — can help slow progression and keep treatment options more conservative. This is one of the reasons routine dental check-ups are encouraged even when no obvious problems are present.
